title: PM Modi Says Poverty Fight Is 'Not Just a Slogan' After World Bank Report
excerpt: Citing the World Bank's October 2026 brief — extreme poverty down to 2.6% — Modi contrasted delivery under his government with the 'Garibi Hatao' era, while the brief's own caveats went unmentioned.
body:
• Prime Minister Narendra Modi, speaking at Ekta Nagar on October 31 and posting on Instagram on November 1, cited the World Bank's October 2026 India brief to argue poverty removal under his government is "not just a slogan."
  • The World Bank brief puts India's extreme poverty at the $3-a-day line at 2.6% in 2023, down from 27.1% in 2011.
  • The brief's separate figure of 496 million people refers to the higher $4.20-a-day line, where poverty fell from 57.7% to 16.1% — a different threshold from the extreme-poverty rate.
  • The same brief carries caveats Modi did not cite: the top 10% of workers earn about 13 times the bottom 10%, and youth unemployment has risen.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi has seized on the World Bank's latest poverty assessment of India to make a political argument: that the fall in poverty under his government is a delivered outcome, not a campaign line. Speaking on Saturday, October 31, at Ekta Nagar in Gujarat during Rashtriya Ekta Diwas — the 151st birth anniversary of Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel — Modi said extreme poverty had fallen from 27 out of every 100 people to fewer than three out of every 100, and turned the figures against the Congress party's historic slogan.

"Since Independence, there has been talk of removing poverty in India. Votes were sought in the name of removing poverty, but we all know the condition of poverty in the country. Those who raised the slogan of 'Garibi Hatao' themselves kept becoming richer."

— Narendra Modi, Prime Minister

Modi returned to the theme on Instagram on November 1, sharing the World Bank findings in a post that began, "A historic fall in poverty. A generational rise in opportunity," with a slide reading, "'Gareebi Hatao' was never a slogan for us. It is our commitment…" The Videshi reported the World Bank data itself when the brief was released; Modi's remarks are the political response to it.

What the World Bank actually reported

The source is the Bank's India Poverty and Equity Brief: October 2026. At the extreme-poverty line of $3.00 a day (2021 purchasing power parity), India's rate fell from 27.1% in 2011 to 2.6% in 2023. At the higher lower-middle-income line of $4.20 a day, the rate fell from 57.7% to 16.1% over the same period — and it is to this second, higher line that the brief's figure of 496 million people moving above the threshold belongs. The two numbers are frequently run together in political speeches and headlines; they measure different things.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=EoDcApoAMRA

The Bank described India's performance in its own words: "Over the past decade, India has made remarkable progress in reducing poverty across both monetary and non-monetary dimensions, recording one of the fastest poverty declines in the world." It credited strong consumption growth, rising employment — up 13.4 crore between 2017 and 2023, especially among women — and expanded social transfers including food subsidies. Electricity access reached 99%.

What Modi credited

In the Ekta Nagar speech, Modi attributed the decline to delivery mechanisms: leakage-free Direct Benefit Transfer, free foodgrain, free healthcare, permanent houses, toilets, clean cooking fuel and insurance coverage. He also said social security coverage had expanded from fewer than 25 crore people before 2014 to nearly 100 crore today. Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman, responding to the brief on October 30, said: "We remain committed to building on this progress through productive employment, stronger household incomes and effective delivery of public services, so that the aspirations of our people are met."

https://x.com/ANI/status/2116531355089809565

The caveats in the same brief

The World Bank brief is not an unqualified endorsement. It notes that the median earnings of the top 10% of workers were about 13 times those of the bottom 10% in 2023, that real earnings were broadly unchanged, and that youth unemployment rose from 14.6% to 15.9% between the first quarters of FY2026 and FY2027, particularly among rural young women. About 57% of India's poor are concentrated in a belt running from Uttar Pradesh to West Bengal. The Bank's estimates rest on the 2011-12 Consumer Expenditure Survey and the 2022-23 and 2023-24 Household Consumption Expenditure Surveys, and the Bank cautions that some of the measured gains may reflect improved measurement. Its indicative projections have the $4.20 poverty rate easing further, to 14.2% in 2026 and 12.1% by 2028.

No opposition or independent-economist reaction to Modi's remarks had been reported by the outlets covering the speech as of publication.
